parts.problem_md:
Which statement correctly describes the contents of the box?

![Diagram showing a mix of single and double circles, with some filled black and others unfilled, randomly arranged against a white background.](assets/001-diagram-showing-a-mix-of-single-and-double-circl.png)
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A / a mixture of elements**

- The box contains two different types of particles that are not chemically bonded together, so it is a **mixture**

  - The unfilled circles represent individual atoms of one **element**
  - The pairs of black circles represent diatomic molecules of another **element**
- Therefore, the box represents a **mixture of two different elements**

**B**, **C**, and **D** are incorrect as the box does not match the descriptions

> **[exam-tip]**
> To answer this type of question, break it down into two steps:
> 
> 1. **Is it a pure substance or a mixture?**
> 
>   - Look at the number of different types of particles
>   - If there is more than one, it is a mixture
>   - This box has two types (single white circles and pairs of black circles), so it is a mixture
> 2. **Are the particles elements or compounds?**
> 
>   - An **element** consists of only one type of atom (e.g., the single white circles, or the pairs of identical black circles).
>   - A **compound** consists of two or more different types of atoms chemically bonded together.
> 
> Since both types of particle in the box are elements, the correct description is a mixture of elements

choices.label: C
choices.text_md: a mixture of elements and compounds

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) How crude oil is separated:

> 
> - The column is heated at the bottom, so is hotter at the bottom and cooler at the top
> - The column has condensers coming off at different heights

parts.problem_md:
An organic compound has the formula (CH<sub>3</sub>COO)<sub>2</sub>Ca

i) Determine the number of different elements in (CH<sub>3</sub>COO)<sub>2</sub>Ca.

[1]

ii) Determine the number of atoms in the formula of (CH<sub>3</sub>COO)<sub>2</sub>Ca.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
i) To determine the number of different elements in (CH<sub>3</sub>COO)<sub>2</sub>Ca:

- Identify the elements present:

carbon (C), hydrogen (H), oxygen (O), and calcium (Ca)

- Count the number of different elements:

There are **4 different elements** **[1 mark]**

ii) To determine the number of atoms in the formula of (CH<sub>3</sub>COO)<sub>2</sub>Ca:

- Find the total number of atoms

  - Remember to multiply everything inside the brackets by the subscript '2'

Carbon (C) atoms = (1 + 1) × 2 = 4

Hydrogen (H) atoms = 3 × 2 = 6

Oxygen (O) atoms = 2 × 2 = 4

Calcium (Ca) atoms = 1

- Add the number of atoms of each element together:

Total atoms = 4 + 6 + 4 + 1

Total atoms = **15 ****[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When you see brackets in a chemical formula followed by a number, like (CH<sub>3</sub>COO)<sub>2</sub>, it means you must multiply the number of every atom inside the bracket by that number.
> 
> A common mistake is to only multiply the last atom in the bracket, or to forget one of the atoms inside. It's good practice to list out each element and count its atoms methodically to avoid errors.

A saturated solution of the salt in 100 g of water is cooled from 60°C to 10°C.

Using your graph, find the mass of salt that crystallises out as the solution cools.

Indicate your working clearly on the graph.
parts.solution_md:
To find the mass of salt that crystallises:

At 10°C:

- Draw a line up from 10°C on the x-axis to the curve
- Draw a line across from the curve to the y-axis
- Read the solubility off at this point

  - This value is 22 g

At 60°C

- Draw a line up from 10°C on the x-axis to the curve
- Draw a line across from the curve to the y-axis
- Read the solubility off at this point

  - This value is 67 g

> 
> 1 mark for subtraction of the two values read from the graph** **
>

parts.problem_md:
When solutions of lead nitrate and potassium sulfate are mixed, one product is solid lead sulfate.

This is the equation for the reaction.

Pb(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2 </sub>(aq) + K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4 </sub>(aq) → PbSO<sub>4 </sub>(s) + 2KNO<sub>3 </sub>(aq)

Identify, at the end of the reaction,

the solute: ............................................

the solvent: ..........................................

the solution: ........................................
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> At the end of the reaction:
> 
> - Solute: potassium nitrate / KNO<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - Solvent: water / H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> - Solution: potassium nitrate / KNO<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A solute is a substance that dissolves in a solvent. The solvent is the liquid that dissolves the solute. The resulting mixture is a solution.
> 
> Notice that a solute does not have to be a solid; it can be a solid, liquid, or gas. For example:
> 
> - In soda water, carbon dioxide gas is the solute.
> - In ethanol solution, ethanol is the solute.

parts.problem_md: Which pair of solutions produces an insoluble salt when mixed?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**

- Common carbonates are insoluble, except for those of sodium, potassium and ammonium
- All nitrates are soluble

  - So, sodium carbonate and calcium nitrate
- The reaction of sodium carbonate and calcium nitrate could form:

  - sodium nitrate
  - calcium carbonate
- Common carbonates are insoluble, except for those of sodium, potassium and ammonium

  - So, calcium carbonate is the insolube product

**A** is incorrect as mixing sodium chloride and potassium chloride solutions would not result in a reaction, as the potential products (KCl and NaCl) are the same as the reactants and both are soluble

**C** is incorrect as both potential products, sodium sulfate (Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) and ammonium chloride (NH<sub>4</sub>Cl), are soluble

**D** is incorrect as both potential products, potassium sulfate (K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) and sodium hydroxide (NaOH), are soluble

> **[exam-tip]**
> To answer this question:
> 
> 1. Predict the products of a double displacement reaction for each pair
> 2. Use the solubility rules to see if either of the products is an insoluble salt

parts.problem_md:
A student investigates the paper chromatography of food colourings using ethanol. Ethanol is a flammable solvent.

![Diagram of a chromatography setup with paper marked by base line and coloured spot. Ethanol level is below the spot in a container.](assets/007-diagram-of-a-chromatography-setup-with-paper-mar.png)

i) State the mobile phase and the stationary phase in the experiment.

[2]

ii) State and explain one safety precaution she should take in the experiment.

[2]

iii) Explain why the level of ethanol should be below the coloured spot at the start of the experiment.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The two phases in the experiment are:
> 
> - Mobile: ethanol **[1 mark]**
> - Stationary: paper **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) A safety precaution to be taken:
> 
> - Keep the experiment away from naked flames** [1 mark]**
> - The ethanol is very flammable **[1 mark]** **OR** Work in a well-ventilated area or fume cupboard **[1 mark]**
> - Ethanol vapour is harmful **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The reason the ethanol level is below the coloured spot:
> 
> - The dyes/colours will dissolve into the solvent and not move up the paper** [1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The stationary phase is the medium that chromatography occurs on. In paper chromatography, this is the **paper**.
> 
> The mobile phase is the solvent that moves up it. In this case, it is **ethanol**.
> 
> For a 2-mark "state and explain" safety question, you must give the **precaution **and then link it to the **specific danger. **
> 
> - Simply stating "it's for safety" is not enough.
> 
> So, the links are:
> 
> - **Ethanol is flammable** so you must **keep it away from flames**.
> - **Ethanol vapour is harmful** so you must **work in a well-ventilated area or fume cupboard**
> 
> Examiner reports often highlight that students lose marks on "why" questions for practical steps. It is not enough to say the spots will dissolve into the solvent. You must explain that this means they will not move up the paper, so no separation will occur.

parts.problem_md:
A different chromatography experiment is set up.

A spot of food colouring is placed on the start line.

A food dye in the colouring has an R<sub>f</sub> value of 0.72

The distance between the start line and the solvent front is 120 mm.

Calculate the distance the food dye moves from the start line.

distance = .............................................................. mm
parts.solution_md:
The distance the food dye moves from the start line is:

- 120 × 0.72; **[1 mark]**
- 86 / 86.4 (mm); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *The R*<sub>*f*</sub>* value is calculated by the equation:*

  - *R*<sub>*f*</sub>* = *$\frac{\mathrm{distance} \mathrm{travelled} \mathrm{by} \mathrm{substance}}{\mathrm{distance} \mathrm{travelled} \mathrm{by} \mathrm{solvent}}$

- *In this question, you are given the R*<sub>*f*</sub>* value but need to calculate the distance travelled by the substance (the food dye)*
- *Substitute the values that you know into the equation for the R*<sub>*f*</sub>* value:*

  - $0.72=\frac{\mathrm{distance} \mathrm{travelled} \mathrm{by} \mathrm{food} \mathrm{dye}}{120}$

- *Rearrange to make the distance travelled by the food dye the subject:*

  - $\mathrm{distance} \mathrm{travelled} \mathrm{by} \mathrm{food} \mathrm{dye}=0.72\times120=86.4$

- *The units will be in mm*

- Heating / boiling the filtrate / solution; **[1 mark]**
- Until crystals form in a cooled sample / on a glass rod 
**OR **
Until the crystallisation point / crystals start to form 
**OR **
Until some of the water has been removed; **[1 mark]**
- Leave the solution to crystallise; **[1 mark]**
- Filter / decant the filtrate / solution; **[1 mark]**
- Dry the crystals between paper towel / in an oven / in a dessicator 
**OR **
Leave the crystals to dry; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *Crystallisation is a common technique covered in longer exam questions*
- *It has some common extra marking points:*

  - *Step 1 - If all of the water is removed from the filtrate / solution, then a maximum of one mark can be awarded*
  - *Step 3 - If the filtrate / solution is completely evaporated, then a maximum of three marks can be awarded*

  - *Until some water boils off*

  - *Dry the crystals*

i) To show that the maximum possible mass of CuSO<sub>4</sub>.5H<sub>2</sub>0 crystals that can be obtained is about 30 g:

Method 1:

- Moles of CuO = $\frac{9.54}{79.5}$ 
**OR **

**OR **
29.94; **[1 mark]**

- *There are two possible approaches to this reacting masses question:*

  1. *The moles approach*
  
    - *Calculating the moles of CuO in 9.54 g *

parts.problem_md:
Chromatography is used to analyse mixtures.

A student does a chromatography experiment to analyse the composition of green food colouring in sweets.

She places four known dyes, A, B, C and D, and the green food colouring on chromatography paper.

The diagram shows the student’s apparatus at the start of her experiment.

![chromatography](assets/030-chromatography.png)

The diagram shows that the student makes two mistakes when setting up her apparatus.

State the two changes that the student should make so that her experiment works.
parts.solution_md:
Two changes the student should make are:

- The level of the water must be below the dyes / start line; **[1 mark]**
- The start line must be drawn in pencil; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *You should be familiar with the set up of a chromatography equipment*
- *The start line must be drawn in pencil as ink will run up the chromatography paper with your sample*
- *If the water is above the dyes, it will cause them to dissolve in the water*

parts.problem_md:
Another student does the chromatography experiment correctly.

The diagram shows her chromatogram at the end of the experiment.

![29ehSO1W_chromatogram](assets/031-29ehso1w-chromatogram.png)

i) Explain what the chromatogram shows about the composition of the green food colouring.

(3)

ii) The distance between the start line and the spot for dye C is 6.2 cm. Calculate the *R*<sub>f</sub> value of dye C.

*R*<sub>f</sub> value = ..............................................................

(3)

iii) Suggest why dye A does not move.

(1)
parts.solution_md:
i)The chromatogram shows:

Any **two** conclusions from:

Dye E:

- Contains (dye) B and (dye) D; **[1 mark]**
- Contains an unknown dye; **[1 mark]**
- Does not contain A or C; **[1 mark]**
- Contains three dyes; **[1 mark]**

Explanation:

- 1 mark for a correct explanation of given conclusion for the green food colouring; **[1 mark]** 
e.g. (explanation for M1) because has spots at same level (as B and D);  
e.g. (explanation for M2) because has a spot at different level (from A B C D) e.g. (explanation for M3) because has no spots at same level (as A and C)

ii) The *R*<sub>f</sub> value is:

- (Distance moved by solvent correctly measured)= 9.5 cm ±2 cm; **[1 mark]**
- Use of equation $\frac{\mathrm{Distance} \mathrm{moved} \mathrm{by} \mathrm{dye}}{\mathrm{Distance} \mathrm{moved} \mathrm{by} \mathrm{solvent}}$; **[1 mark]** 
e.g. $\frac{6.2}{9.5}$
- Evaluation of *R*<sub>f</sub>; **[1 mark]** 
e.g. $\frac{6.2}{9.5}=0.65(3)$

iii) Dye A does not move because:

- It is not soluble in water; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 7 marks]**

- *To determine which dyes are present in the green food colouring, look to see whether the dots are horizontally in line with one another, in this case, B and D*
- *The number of dots for the green food colouring indicates the total number of dyes present*
- *In the case of the green food colouring, there are three dots so the substance contains three dyes and is a mixture*
- *One dot would indicate the sample is pure*
- *When the solvent moves over the dyes, they will dissolve in the solvent and be carried up the paper*
- *If the sample has not moved, this is due to it not being soluble in that particular solvent, sometimes a different solvent can be used *
- *You must learn the equation to calculate the **R*<sub>*f*</sub>* value, and remember, your answer should always be less than 1*
- *Make sure you read the question carefully, as sometimes you could be asked to provide the distances moved by the solvent and dyes in mm *
